json.title: Questions to Ask a Potential Co-Parent Before You Move Forward
json.excerpt: Thinking about co-parenting with someone? These practical questions can help you talk about parenting, money, living arrangements, boundaries and the future.
json.content:
Start with the life you both imagine

Before you get into practical details, talk about the bigger picture.

What does family mean to you? What made you decide that you want a child? What do you imagine your life looking like five years after becoming a parent?

You may discover that you agree on the important things. You may also discover that you have completely different ideas of what family life should look like.

Neither outcome is necessarily a problem. The important part is knowing about those differences before you make commitments.

What does co-parenting actually mean to each of you?

Two people can use the word co-parenting and imagine very different arrangements.

For one person, it may mean an equal split of time. For another, it may mean living separately while one parent has the child most weekdays. Someone else may imagine a close friendship between two households.

Ask each other to describe a normal week.

Where would the child wake up? Who would take them to school or childcare? How often would they see each parent? How would holidays work?

Concrete examples are often more revealing than broad statements like “We'll share everything.”

Where would the child live?

This can become one of the biggest practical questions, especially if you live in different neighbourhoods or cities.

Would the child have two homes? How close would they need to be? Would one parent move if necessary? What happens if one of you gets a job somewhere else?

You don't need to solve every future scenario. But you should understand whether your expectations are fundamentally compatible.

Distance can also affect school, childcare, friendships and the amount of everyday time each parent can realistically spend with the child.

How will you make decisions?

Co-parenting means making decisions together, sometimes when you strongly disagree.

Talk about healthcare, education, childcare, religion, language, travel and extracurricular activities.

Then go one step further: what happens when you don't agree?

Will you try to reach consensus? Will certain decisions belong to one parent? Would you use mediation if you reach an impasse?

There is no single model that works for every family. What matters is that you have a way of handling disagreement before the disagreement arrives.

What does money look like?

Money can be uncomfortable to discuss with someone you barely know. It is also one of the conversations worth having early.

How would pregnancy and fertility-related costs be handled? What about childcare, clothing, healthcare, school activities, travel and unexpected expenses?

Would expenses be split equally or according to income? What happens if one parent earns significantly more than the other?

You don't need a perfect financial plan before you meet a potential co-parent. But avoiding the subject because it feels awkward is rarely a good sign.

What happens if one of you gets a new partner?

This is one of the questions people often postpone because it feels hypothetical.

But it isn't difficult to imagine. One of you may eventually fall in love, marry, move in with someone or have another child.

How would a new partner fit into your child's life? What boundaries would you want? Who would make decisions? Would a new partner ever be involved in childcare?

You don't need to predict who that person will be. You do need to know whether both of you can accept that your lives will continue to change.

What are your boundaries?

Good co-parenting doesn't require you to be close friends. It does require clear boundaries.

How much communication do you expect? How often would you contact each other? Would you share personal details about new relationships? How would you handle conflict?

Ask yourself a quieter question, too: can you comfortably tell this person “no”?

If you already feel pressure to agree because you are afraid of losing the opportunity to become a parent, that's something worth taking seriously.

How do you think about the child's relationship with each parent?

Talk about what you want your child to experience, rather than only what you want as adults.

Would you both be actively involved? How would you handle a period when the child strongly prefers one parent? What if the child asks why you don't live together?

If donor conception is involved, talk about how you would approach the child's questions about their origins. Professional guidance increasingly emphasises thoughtful, age-appropriate communication about donor conception rather than treating it as something that must remain hidden.

The goal isn't to script your child's future feelings. It is to make sure the adults are prepared to respond openly and consistently.

How do you handle conflict?

This may be the most important question of all, and you can learn a lot without creating an artificial test.

Notice what happens when you disagree.

Does the person listen? Do they interrupt? Do they become defensive? Can they change their mind? Do they apologise when they have gone too far?

Everyone gets frustrated. Co-parenting doesn't require perfect emotional control.

It does require a relationship in which conflict can eventually come back down to a conversation about what is best for the child.

What would make you walk away?

It can be surprisingly useful to discuss this directly.

What would make each of you decide that co-parenting is no longer a good idea? What concerns would need to be addressed before moving forward?

This conversation gives both people permission to say that something doesn't feel right.

That matters because the desire to become a parent can be powerful enough to make people minimise concerns they would normally take seriously.

Don't make the questions feel like an interview

You don't need to ask all of these questions on the first date.

In fact, you probably shouldn't.

Let the conversations develop. Ask something, listen to the answer, and come back to the subject later. See whether the person's views stay consistent. Pay attention to how they respond when you disagree.

You are not trying to collect the “right” answers.

You are trying to understand whether the two of you can build a relationship in which difficult questions can be asked safely.

Before you move forward

If the conversations are going well, there is still no need to rush.

Talk to a professional where it makes sense. A fertility specialist can answer medical questions. A psychologist can help you explore expectations, boundaries and the emotional side of the arrangement. An independent lawyer can explain the legal position in your country.

This is particularly important if donor conception or fertility treatment is involved. In the UK, for example, legal parenthood can depend on specific consent requirements when treatment involves donated sperm or embryos, and private donor arrangements can have different legal consequences. The rules are not universal, so advice should be specific to your circumstances.

And remember: a good conversation is not a promise.

You are allowed to keep getting to know someone. You are allowed to change your mind. You are allowed to say that the match doesn't feel right.

A better question than “Are we compatible?”

Instead of asking whether you and a potential co-parent are compatible, try asking something more useful:

“Can we handle the difficult parts together?”

You don't need identical personalities. You don't need the same hobbies. You don't even need to agree on everything.

You need enough shared values, trust and communication to make decisions when life doesn't go according to plan.

That is what you are really looking for.

Not a perfect person.

A workable relationship.

A simple way to use these questions

Save the questions and return to them over several conversations rather than trying to cover everything at once. You can also write down your own answers first. That makes it easier to notice where you have firm boundaries and where you are genuinely open to compromise.

Explore co-parenting with LetsBeParents

If you're exploring co-parenting, LetsBeParents is being built to give people a more thoughtful place to meet others considering the same path, while making it easier to find professional support when medical, psychological or legal questions come up.
